content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Jennifer Martin (E033) requests admin access to Payroll.

Six notes. Five notes say she's an Analyst, full-time. One note (Security) says she's a contractor with basic security training.

The discrepancy: employment type. Five notes say full-time; one says contractor.

The policy:
- full_time: up to write; admin only if role owns system (Payroll owned by Payroll Specialist role; she's Analyst, so no admin).
- contractor: read, or write if advanced security training; never admin.

Either way, admin is not allowed. For full-time Analyst, max is write. For contractor with basic training, max is read.

So maximum is either write (if full-time) or read (if contractor). Requested is admin, above max either way. Grant max.

But which max? There's conflicting info. The majority (5 notes) say full-time Analyst → max write. The security note says contractor with basic training → max read.

Hmm, as the Approver, I need to make the final decision. Given conflicting evidence, the majority of sources say full-time. The Security note says it differs from other notes. 

Which to trust? Let's think. The security database might be authoritative for employment type? Or HR? Typically HR is authoritative for employment type. Note 1 is presumably HR (it didn't specify which agent, but "role: Analyst, employment type: full_time" and recommendation). Actually the notes don't label which agent wrote each except by content: IT database (note 2), Finance (3), Compliance (4), Facilities (5), Security (6). Note 1 might be HR.

Five databases confirm full-time. One (Security) says contractor. The security note itself acknowledges it differs.

Given the majority consensus and that HR typically owns employment type facts, I'd lean full-time → max write. But there's a conflict. The safest approach: grant the lower of the two maxima? Hmm.

Policy says never grant more than requested. Requested is admin. Max is either write or read. Granting write when the employee is actually a contractor with basic training would violate policy (granting more than allowed). Granting read when employee is full-time would be under-granting but within policy? Actually granting read when max is write is allowed? The policy says never grant more than requested, and grant requested if at or below max, else grant max. If the employee is full-time, max is write, so they'd be entitled to write; granting read is below what they're entitled to but not violating "never more than requested"? It would grant less than the max. For access requests, granting less is usually safe/conservative.

But we should decide based on evidence. The majority evidence strongly indicates full-time Analyst. Five notes vs one. I'll go with full-time → max write.

Actually, let me reconsider. The security team's database might have the most accurate employment-type info? No - employment type is an HR fact. The consensus is full-time.

Given five independent sources (HR, IT, Finance, Compliance, Facilities) all say full-time Analyst, and only security differs, I'll decide the employee is full-time. Max = write. Requested admin > write, so grant write.

Let me submit decision: write.

Reason: Jennifer Martin (E033) is a full-time Analyst per HR/IT/Finance/Compliance/Facilities records. Payroll is owned by the Payroll Specialist role, so admin is not permitted for an Analyst. Full-time maximum is write; requested admin exceeds max, so grant write. (Security note lists contractor, but five sources agree on full-time; either way admin is not allowed.)
